rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.4 - two-season greenhouse field experiment on cucumber in red clay soil with a two-factor randomized block design (three dissolved-oxygen levels of micro-nano bubble water delivered by subsurface drip, three biochar rates, plus CK), own measurements of soil, plant, yield and quality variables. Q2: Section 3.6 and Fig. 9 - DO concentration in MNBW had a highly significant effect on cucumber yield (P<0.01) and yield rose significantly as DO concentration increased; IWUE and WUE also rose with DO; Section 3.6 - vitamin C and sugar-acid ratio affected by DO level, organic acid decreased with DO. O1 (4-5 mg/L) is the natural non-aerated DO, so the DO factor compares aerated with conventional drip water. Q4: Section 3.1/Fig. 3 - soil oxygen and redox potential increased significantly with DO in MNBW; Section 3.4/Fig. 7 - net photosynthetic rate increased with DO; Section 3.5 - dry matter rose; Section 3.7/Fig. 10 - soil oxygen, aeration porosity, Pn and dry weight positively correlated with yield (P<0.05), i.e. the intermediate variables (root-zone oxygen, photosynthesis) were measured.
rows.notes: Only the yield and quality parts of the passage are supported. The study has no data on pesticide applications or on nutrient-element consumption. The CK has no biochar while all aerated treatments include biochar (20-60 t/hm2), so the aeration effect is isolated only via the DO main effect within biochar treatments, not via a pure aerated-vs-non-aerated comparison against CK. Single site, soil, crop and greenhouse; two seasons. Uncertainty reported only as letter groupings, P-values and ranges of percentage increases across treatments; no SD/CI given in text. No limitations stated beyond 'more research' on mechanisms.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.4 - two-season greenhouse experiment with own measurements of soil aeration, plant growth, photosynthesis, dry matter, yield and fruit quality.
rows.notes: The study does not measure pesticide use, pest or disease incidence, or anything related to pest control. It reports effects of micro-nano bubble water DO level and biochar on soil aeration, photosynthesis, dry matter, yield, WUE and fruit quality (VC, organic acid, sugar-acid ratio) of greenhouse cucumber. No evidence for reduced pesticide applications.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.4 - own two-season greenhouse field experiment on cucumber with micro-nano bubble water (three DO levels) via subsurface drip and biochar rates. Q2: Section 3.3/Fig. 6 - plant height and stem diameter significantly affected by DO in MNBW (P<0.01); Section 3.4/Fig. 7 - Pn significantly increased with DO concentration; Section 3.5/Fig. 8 - root, stem, leaf and total dry weight increased significantly with DO in MNBW; Section 3.6/Fig. 9 - yield, IWUE and WUE rose significantly with DO level; Abstract - yield increased 1.72-44.23 % and WUE 0.42-76.57 % relative to CK. Q4: Section 3.1/Fig. 3 - soil oxygen and redox potential measured and shown to rise with DO in MNBW; Section 3.7/Fig. 10 - SO, SAP and Pn positively correlated with dry weight and yield, i.e. the root-zone oxygen and photosynthetic pathway was measured.
rows.notes: Aeration effect is derived from the DO main effect in a factorial design in which every aerated treatment also received biochar; CK (no biochar, natural DO) is not a clean aerated-vs-non-aerated contrast. Single site, soil and crop, two seasons in one greenhouse. Dispersion reported only via letter groupings/P-values and treatment ranges. Only 'more research' noted as limitation.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.4 - own two-season greenhouse experiment with soil aeration (bulk density, porosity, aeration porosity, redox potential, soil oxygen), soil moisture, temperature and conductivity measured by sensors and ring-knife sampling. Q2: Section 3.1/Fig. 3 - both the biochar amount and the DO concentration in MNBW significantly raised soil redox potential and soil oxygen (P<0.01), with a significant interaction; Section 4.1 - soil oxygen increased 0.47-31.80 % and redox potential 0.54-34.74 % across treatments relative to CK; Conclusions - oxygen-rich MNBW greatly raised soil redox potential and oxygen content.
rows.notes: Only soil oxygen and redox potential responded to aeration; DO level had no significant effect on bulk density, porosity, aeration porosity or soil water content (Sections 3.1, 3.2) - those improvements came from biochar. Q4 answered no because the DO in irrigation water is the treatment variable itself rather than a measured intermediate; the mechanism (bubble half-life, mass transfer) is only cited in Discussion 4.1. Single site, soil, crop; no dispersion statistics beyond letter groupings and ranges; no stated limitations.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Figures are not reproduced, so whether error bars are shown cannot be checked; the text reports only P-values, Duncan letter groupings and ranges of percentage change across treatments.
